```{r packages}
library(tidyverse)   # readr, dplyr, tidyr, stringr, ggplot2
library(knitr)       # kable() tables
library(broom)       # tidy() and glance() model summaries

YEARS      <- 2022:2025
AGE_LEVELS <- c("13-19", "20-39", "40-59", "60+")
```

# Introduction

Many people know exercise is important, yet not everyone acts on it. ActiveSG data show that from 2022 to 2025, gym visits by
women grew much faster than men's, and those by adults aged 60+ grew fastest.

**Research question:** How do motivations and barriers to exercise relate to
changing ActiveSG gym attendance across age and sex between 2022 and 2025?

Following the instructor's feedback on our proposal, we analyse groups, divide
visits by population, use four survey indices and check for Simpson's paradox.

# 1. Datasets and data preparation

## 1a. Observations and variables

We use three public datasets (Department of Statistics Singapore, n.d.;
Sport Singapore, n.d.-a, n.d.-b, 2026).

```{r load}
mot_raw <- read_csv("MotivationstoParticipateinSportExercise.csv")
bar_raw <- read_csv("BarrierstoParticipationinSportExercise.csv")

# The SingStat file has notes above and below the table; readLines() + read.csv()
# keeps the leading spaces in "Data Series", which mark region, sex and age rows.
gym_lines <- readLines("M920481.csv", warn = FALSE)
header    <- grep("^Data Series", gym_lines)
gym_raw   <- read.csv(text = gym_lines[header:length(gym_lines)],
                      colClasses = "character", check.names = FALSE,
                      strip.white = FALSE)
names(gym_raw) <- trimws(names(gym_raw))
gym_raw <- gym_raw |>
  filter(!is.na(suppressWarnings(as.numeric(`2025`))))   # keep data rows only

tibble(Dataset      = c("Motivations survey", "Barriers survey", "ActiveSG gym visits"),
       Observations = c(nrow(mot_raw), nrow(bar_raw), nrow(gym_raw)),
       Variables    = c(ncol(mot_raw), ncol(bar_raw), ncol(gym_raw)),
       Years        = c("2019-2025", "2019-2025", "2022-2025")) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, caption = "Size of each dataset")
```

Each survey row gives the % citing one reason in one year, age group and sex
(motivations: participants; barriers: non-participants). The gym table has one row per region, sex or age series.

## 1b. Variable types

```{r var-types}
var_types <- function(data, name) {
  tibble(Dataset = name, Variable = names(data),
         Type = map_chr(data, ~ class(.x)[1]))
}

bind_rows(var_types(mot_raw, "Motivations"),
          var_types(bar_raw, "Barriers"),
          var_types(gym_raw, "Gym visits")) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, caption = "Variable types in the raw datasets")
```

Year and Percentage are numeric; age group, sex and reason are categorical.
Gym visit counts are read as text and converted below.

## 1c. Data preparation

**Harmonising age groups.** The same group appears as "13 to 19", "13 -19" and
"13 - 19", so we remove spaces and replace "to" with "-".

```{r clean-age}
clean_age <- function(x) str_replace(str_remove_all(x, "\\s"), "to", "-")
```

**Survey indices.** Four indices, chosen before modelling, combine related
items: health motivation (physical or mental health), enjoyment motivation
(interest in the sport or meeting people), time barriers (work, family, school)
and health barriers (too old or health condition). The surveys publish only
each group's top 10 items, so a missing item is coded 0, a lower bound rather
than an observed value (table below; Section 4c tests this).

```{r survey-indices}
mot_items <- c(physical = "better physical health", mental = "better mental health",
               interest = "interest of the sports", social = "meet other people")
bar_items <- c(overtime = "too busy working overtime", family = "take care of family members",
               school = "too busy with schoolwork", studywork = "studying and working",
               twojobs = "more than one job", too_old = "too old for sport",
               health_cnd = "health condition is not suitable")

# For each item, find its rows and place the % in a 32-row grid (NA = not in top 10)
extract_items <- function(df, item_col, patterns) {
  df <- df |>
    rename(item = all_of(item_col)) |>
    filter(Year %in% YEARS) |>
    mutate(AgeGroup = clean_age(AgeGroup), item = str_to_lower(item))
  grid <- expand_grid(Year = YEARS, AgeGroup = AGE_LEVELS, Sex = c("Female", "Male"))
  for (nm in names(patterns)) {
    matched <- df |>
      filter(str_detect(item, fixed(patterns[[nm]]))) |>
      group_by(Year, AgeGroup, Sex) |>
      summarise(!!nm := sum(Percentage), .groups = "drop")
    grid <- left_join(grid, matched, by = c("Year", "AgeGroup", "Sex"))
  }
  grid
}

items <- extract_items(mot_raw, "Motivations", mot_items) |>
  left_join(extract_items(bar_raw, "Barriers", bar_items),
            by = c("Year", "AgeGroup", "Sex"))

item_labels <- c(
  physical = "M: better physical health", mental = "M: better mental health",
  interest = "M: interest in the sport", social = "M: meet other people",
  overtime = "B: busy working overtime", family = "B: care for family",
  school = "B: busy with schoolwork", studywork = "B: studying and working",
  twojobs = "B: more than one job", too_old = "B: too old for sport",
  health_cnd = "B: health condition")

items |>
  summarise(across(-c(Year, AgeGroup, Sex), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Item", values_to = "Cells set to 0 (of 32)") |>
  mutate(Item = item_labels[Item]) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, caption = "Survey items missing from a group's top 10")

items <- items |> mutate(across(-c(Year, AgeGroup, Sex), ~ replace_na(.x, 0)))

survey <- items |>
  transmute(Year, AgeGroup, Sex,
            mot_health = (physical + mental) / 2,                      # % of participants
            mot_enjoy  = (interest + social) / 2,
            bar_time   = overtime + family + school + studywork + twojobs,  # per 100 non-participants
            bar_health = too_old + health_cnd)
```

**Gym visits.** The table marks region, sex and age rows only by indentation,
so we count leading spaces, carry labels down with `fill()`, and sum over the
five regions.

```{r parse-gym}
gym_long <- gym_raw |>
  rename(series = `Data Series`) |>
  mutate(indent = nchar(series) - nchar(trimws(series, which = "left")),
         label  = trimws(series),
         region = if_else(indent == 0, label, NA_character_),
         sex    = if_else(indent == 2, label, NA_character_)) |>
  fill(region) |>
  group_by(region) |> fill(sex) |> ungroup() |>
  pivot_longer(as.character(YEARS), names_to = "Year", values_to = "visits") |>
  mutate(Year = as.integer(Year), visits = as.numeric(visits))
```

**The 2024 gap.** About 1.47 million visits in July–December 2024 have no
region, sex or age. We allocate them by each group's share of recorded 2024
visits; otherwise 2024 would show a false drop.

```{r gap-2024}
year_totals <- gym_long |>
  filter(indent == 0) |>
  group_by(Year) |>
  summarise(grand_total = sum(visits))

age_sex <- gym_long |>
  filter(indent == 4, sex %in% c("Female", "Male"),
         label %in% c("13 - 19", "20 - 39", "40 - 59", "60+")) |>
  mutate(AgeGroup = clean_age(label)) |>
  group_by(Year, AgeGroup, Sex = sex) |>
  summarise(visits_recorded = sum(visits), .groups = "drop")

allocation <- age_sex |>
  group_by(Year) |>
  summarise(recorded = sum(visits_recorded)) |>
  left_join(year_totals, by = "Year") |>
  mutate(scale_factor = grand_total / recorded)

allocation |>
  mutate(Year = as.character(Year)) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, digits = 3, format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
        caption = "Allocation of visits with no age or sex recorded")
```

**Visits per resident.** Total visits largely reflect group size, so we divide
by each group's resident population (SingStat table M810011, end June). The
13–19 population is two-fifths of the 10–14 band (assuming ages are evenly
spread) plus the 15–19 band.

```{r merge}
population <- read_csv("population.csv")

merged <- age_sex |>
  left_join(select(allocation, Year, scale_factor), by = "Year") |>
  mutate(visits = visits_recorded * scale_factor) |>
  inner_join(survey, by = c("Year", "AgeGroup", "Sex")) |>
  left_join(population, by = c("Year", "AgeGroup", "Sex")) |>
  mutate(year  = Year,
         age   = factor(AgeGroup, levels = AGE_LEVELS),
         sex   = factor(Sex, levels = c("Female", "Male")),
         group = paste(AgeGroup, Sex),
         visits_per_resident = visits / Population) |>
  select(year, age, sex, group, visits, population = Population,
         visits_per_resident, mot_health, mot_enjoy, bar_time, bar_health)

stopifnot(nrow(merged) == 32, !anyNA(merged))
glimpse(merged)
```

The final dataset has 32 rows (4 years × 4 age groups × 2 sexes) and
`r ncol(merged)` variables: age group and sex are categorical; all others are
numeric.

# 2. Summary statistics

```{r stats-helper}
stats5 <- function(data, var) {
  data |> summarise(n = n(), Mean = mean({{ var }}), Median = median({{ var }}),
                    SD = sd({{ var }}), Min = min({{ var }}), Max = max({{ var }}))
}
tab <- function(x, cap, d = 2) kable(x, booktabs = TRUE, digits = d,
                                     format.args = list(big.mark = ","), caption = cap)
```

```{r stats-visits}
bind_rows(merged |> stats5(visits) |> mutate(Year = "All years"),
          merged |> group_by(Year = year) |> stats5(visits) |> mutate(Year = as.character(Year))) |>
  relocate(Year) |>
  tab("Annual gym visits per age-sex group", d = 0)

bind_rows(merged |> group_by(Group = sex) |> stats5(visits_per_resident),
          merged |> group_by(Group = age) |> stats5(visits_per_resident)) |>
  mutate(Group = as.character(Group)) |>
  tab("Gym visits per resident by sex and age group")
```

Visits are right-skewed (mean `r format(round(mean(merged$visits)), big.mark = ",")`,
median `r format(round(median(merged$visits)), big.mark = ",")`): a few large groups,
especially men aged 20–39, pull the mean up. Per resident, men made about four
times as many visits as women (2.40 vs 0.59 a year), and use falls steadily
with age, from 3.16 visits per teenager to 0.49 among those aged 60+.

```{r stats-survey}
items |>
  pivot_longer(-c(Year, AgeGroup, Sex), names_to = "Item", values_to = "pct") |>
  mutate(Item = item_labels[Item]) |>
  group_by(Item) |> stats5(pct) |> arrange(desc(Mean)) |>
  tab("Survey items (% of respondents)", d = 1)

merged |>
  pivot_longer(mot_health:bar_health, names_to = "Index", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(Index = recode(Index, mot_health = "Health motivation", mot_enjoy = "Enjoyment motivation",
                        bar_time = "Time barrier", bar_health = "Health barrier")) |>
  group_by(Index, `Age group` = age) |> stats5(value) |>
  tab("Motivation and barrier indices by age group", d = 1)
```

Better physical health is the most common motivation (mean 79%); overtime
and family care are the most common barriers. Age, not sex, divides the
indices: enjoyment motivation falls from 38 (teenagers) to 10 (60+), while
health barriers rise from under 12 to 60.

# 3. Visualisations

```{r chart1, fig.height = 3.2}
merged |>
  group_by(year, sex) |> summarise(visits = sum(visits), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(sex) |> mutate(index = visits / visits[year == 2022] * 100) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, index, colour = sex)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(title = "Chart 1. Female gym visits doubled between 2022 and 2025",
       x = "Year", y = "Visits index (2022 = 100)", colour = "Sex") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Female visits grew much faster than male visits** (+103% vs +59%), and the growth gap
widened after 2023, when male visits plateaued.

```{r chart2, fig.height = 2.8}
merged |>
  filter(year %in% c(2022, 2025)) |>
  select(year, age, sex, visits) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = visits, names_prefix = "y") |>
  mutate(growth = (y2025 / y2022 - 1) * 100) |>
  ggplot(aes(age, growth, fill = sex)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(growth), "%")),
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.9), vjust = -0.3, size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Chart 2. Older groups grew fastest; 60+ women tripled their visits",
       x = "Age group", y = "Growth in visits, 2022-2025 (%)", fill = "Sex") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Growth rises with age for both sexes**, from 37% (men) and 71% (women) among
teenagers to 121% and 201% among those aged 60+.

```{r chart3, fig.height = 3.2}
merged |>
  group_by(age) |>
  summarise(Time = mean(bar_time), Health = mean(bar_health)) |>
  pivot_longer(-age, names_to = "barrier", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(age, value, fill = barrier)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(title = "Chart 3. Time barriers dominate under 60; health barriers dominate 60+",
       x = "Age group", y = "Mentions per 100 non-participants", fill = "Barrier") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Health, not time, is the main barrier after 60.** Time barriers peak at about
75 mentions per 100 among 20–39 year olds and fall to 17 at 60+.

```{r chart4, fig.height = 3.2}
merged |>
  group_by(age, sex) |>
  summarise(Health = mean(mot_health), Enjoyment = mean(mot_enjoy), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_longer(c(Health, Enjoyment), names_to = "motivation", values_to = "pct") |>
  ggplot(aes(age, pct, colour = motivation, group = motivation)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ sex) +
  labs(title = "Chart 4. Enjoyment motivation fades with age; health motivation rises",
       x = "Age group", y = "% of participants", colour = "Motivation") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Motivation shifts from enjoyment to health with age.** Enjoyment falls from
about 43% to 9% among men and from 34% to 12% among women.

```{r chart5, fig.height = 3.8}
ggplot(merged, aes(bar_health, log(visits_per_resident))) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = group)) +
  geom_smooth(aes(colour = group), method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "black", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Chart 5. The pooled trend (dashed) reverses within groups",
       x = "Health barrier index", y = "log(gym visits per resident)", colour = "Group") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**The pooled trend is misleading.** Across all groups, higher health barriers
go with fewer visits per resident, but within six of eight age-sex groups the link is
positive. The pooled line compares older with younger groups: a
Simpson's paradox.

# 4. Models

```{r model-data}
gym <- merged |>
  mutate(year = factor(year),
         male = as.integer(sex == "Male"),
         log_vpr = log(visits_per_resident),
         across(mot_health:bar_health, ~ as.numeric(scale(.x))))   # z-scores
```

The outcome is log(visits per resident), because the rates are right-skewed.
Indices are z-scores, so a coefficient *b* means the visit rate changes by
100 × (e^b^ − 1)% per 1 SD increase.

## 4a. Two models and their motivation

```{r simpson-check, include=FALSE}
simpson_pooled <- coef(lm(log_vpr ~ mot_health, data = gym))[["mot_health"]]
simpson_pos <- gym |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(slope = coef(lm(log_vpr ~ mot_health))[["mot_health"]]) |>
  summarise(n = sum(slope > 0)) |>
  pull(n)
```

As Chart 5 shows, comparing groups mainly compares young and old people:
health motivation's uncontrolled slope is also negative
(`r round(simpson_pooled, 2)`) but positive within `r simpson_pos` of 8 groups.
Both models therefore control for age-sex group and year, comparing each group
only with itself.

**Model 1 (control model).** Is a group's gym use higher in years when its
motivations are stronger or barriers weaker? It adds age-sex group
(removing stable differences) and year (removing shared changes such as
post-COVID recovery) to the four indices.

```{r model-1}
model_1 <- lm(log_vpr ~ mot_health + mot_enjoy + bar_time + bar_health +
                group + year, data = gym)
summary(model_1)
```

**Model 2 (interaction model).** Our question asks how links differ by sex, so
Model 2 adds one interaction, enjoyment × sex. Only one is tested, as 32 rows
cannot support more.

```{r model-2}
model_2 <- lm(log_vpr ~ mot_health + mot_enjoy + bar_time + bar_health +
                mot_enjoy:male + group + year, data = gym)
summary(model_2)
```

## 4b. Can the models be compared?

Yes. Both use the same outcome and 32 rows, and Model 1 is nested in Model 2,
so adjusted R², AIC and an F-test apply.

```{r compare}
bind_rows(glance(model_1) |> mutate(model = "Model 1: control"),
          glance(model_2) |> mutate(model = "Model 2: + enjoyment x sex")) |>
  select(model, r.squared, adj.r.squared, sigma, AIC, df.residual, nobs) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, digits = 3, caption = "Model fit")

f_test <- anova(model_1, model_2)
f_test
```

## 4c. Which is the better model?

```{r fit-plot, fig.height = 3.4}
bind_rows(
  gym |> mutate(model = "Model 1: control", predicted = fitted(model_1)),
  gym |> mutate(model = "Model 2: + enjoyment x sex", predicted = fitted(model_2))) |>
  ggplot(aes(predicted, log_vpr, colour = age, shape = sex)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  labs(title = "Observed vs predicted log(visits per resident)",
       subtitle = "Points on the dashed line are predicted perfectly",
       x = "Predicted", y = "Observed", colour = "Age group", shape = "Sex") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r resid-plot, fig.height = 3.4}
bind_rows(
  gym |> mutate(model = "Model 1: control",
                fitted = fitted(model_1), residual = resid(model_1)),
  gym |> mutate(model = "Model 2: + enjoyment x sex",
                fitted = fitted(model_2), residual = resid(model_2))) |>
  ggplot(aes(fitted, residual, colour = age, shape = sex)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  labs(title = "Residuals of each model",
       x = "Fitted log(visits per resident)", y = "Residual",
       colour = "Age group", shape = "Sex") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r numbers, include=FALSE}
pct  <- function(b) round(100 * (exp(b) - 1))
ptxt <- function(p) if (p < 0.001) "p < 0.001" else paste0("p = ", formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 3))
pval <- function(m, term) ptxt(summary(m)$coefficients[term, "Pr(>|t|)"])
f_p  <- ptxt(f_test[["Pr(>F)"]][2])

b <- coef(model_2); V <- vcov(model_2)
slope_women <- b[["mot_enjoy"]]
slope_men   <- b[["mot_enjoy"]] + b[["mot_enjoy:male"]]
se_men      <- sqrt(V["mot_enjoy", "mot_enjoy"] + V["mot_enjoy:male", "mot_enjoy:male"] +
                    2 * V["mot_enjoy", "mot_enjoy:male"])
p_men       <- ptxt(2 * pt(-abs(slope_men / se_men), df.residual(model_2)))
```

```{r checks}
# Check 1: do the four indices add to a group + year baseline?
model_0 <- lm(log_vpr ~ group + year, data = gym)
p_base  <- ptxt(anova(model_0, model_1)[["Pr(>F)"]][2])

# Check 2: fill items missing from the top 10 with each group's 10th-ranked value
fill_tenth <- function(raw, item_col, patterns) {
  tenth <- raw |>
    filter(Year %in% YEARS) |>
    mutate(AgeGroup = clean_age(AgeGroup)) |>
    group_by(Year, AgeGroup, Sex) |>
    summarise(tenth = min(Percentage), .groups = "drop")
  extract_items(raw, item_col, patterns) |>
    left_join(tenth, by = c("Year", "AgeGroup", "Sex")) |>
    mutate(across(all_of(names(patterns)), ~ coalesce(.x, tenth))) |>
    select(-tenth)
}

survey_sens <- fill_tenth(mot_raw, "Motivations", mot_items) |>
  left_join(fill_tenth(bar_raw, "Barriers", bar_items), by = c("Year", "AgeGroup", "Sex")) |>
  transmute(year = factor(Year), age = AgeGroup, sex = Sex,
            mot_health = (physical + mental) / 2,
            mot_enjoy  = (interest + social) / 2,
            bar_time   = overtime + family + school + studywork + twojobs,
            bar_health = too_old + health_cnd) |>
  mutate(across(mot_health:bar_health, ~ as.numeric(scale(.x))))

gym_sens <- gym |>
  select(-(mot_health:bar_health)) |>
  mutate(age = as.character(age), sex = as.character(sex)) |>
  left_join(survey_sens, by = c("year", "age", "sex"))

model_1_sens <- update(model_1, data = gym_sens)
model_2_sens <- update(model_2, data = gym_sens)
```

Model 2 is better: adjusted R² rises from
`r round(summary(model_1)$adj.r.squared, 3)` to
`r round(summary(model_2)$adj.r.squared, 3)`, AIC falls from
`r round(AIC(model_1), 1)` to `r round(AIC(model_2), 1)`, the F-test is
significant (`r f_p`), and its residuals are smaller. However, the interaction
was chosen after exploring the data, so the result is tentative.

Two checks support the indices: adding them to a group-and-year baseline
improves fit (`r p_base`), and filling missing top-10 items with each group's
10th-ranked value (their maximum) instead of 0 barely changes the results
(enjoyment +`r pct(coef(model_1_sens)[["mot_enjoy"]])`%,
`r pval(model_1_sens, "mot_enjoy")`; interaction
`r pval(model_2_sens, "mot_enjoy:male")`).

## 4d. Interpreting the results

```{r coefficients, fig.height = 3.4}
coefs <- bind_rows(tidy(model_1, conf.int = TRUE) |> mutate(model = "Model 1: control"),
                   tidy(model_2, conf.int = TRUE) |> mutate(model = "Model 2: + enjoyment x sex")) |>
  filter(term %in% c("mot_health", "mot_enjoy", "bar_time", "bar_health", "mot_enjoy:male")) |>
  mutate(term = recode(term, mot_health = "Health motivation", mot_enjoy = "Enjoyment motivation",
                       bar_time = "Time barrier", bar_health = "Health barrier",
                       `mot_enjoy:male` = "Enjoyment x male"))

ggplot(coefs, aes(estimate, term, colour = model)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high),
                  position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  labs(title = "Coefficients with 95% confidence intervals",
       x = "Change in log(visits per resident) per 1 SD", y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

- **Model 1.** Comparing each group with itself, enjoyment motivation stands out: in years when
  a group's enjoyment index was 1 SD higher, its visit rate was about
  `r pct(coef(model_1)[["mot_enjoy"]])`% higher (`r pval(model_1, "mot_enjoy")`).
  Health motivation shows at most a weak link (`r pval(model_1, "mot_health")`)
  and time barriers none (`r pval(model_1, "bar_time")`). The health barrier is
  positive (`r pct(coef(model_1)[["bar_health"]])`%,
  `r pval(model_1, "bar_health")`), which is counter-intuitive; as barriers
  come from non-participants, we do not read this as an effect.
- **Model 2.** The enjoyment link may be stronger for women (about
  `r pct(slope_women)`% per 1 SD, `r pval(model_2, "mot_enjoy")`) than for men
  (about `r pct(slope_men)`%, `r p_men`); the difference is significant
  (`r pval(model_2, "mot_enjoy:male")`) but exploratory.
- **In plain English.** Gym use per resident was higher in years when more
  people in a group said they exercise for enjoyment and to meet others,
  possibly more so among women.

# Limitations

Results are group-level associations, not individual or causal effects.
Motivations and barriers come from different respondents, visits include repeat
visits, and the surveys cover sport generally, not only gyms.
